alt: A one-metre square is 100 cm along each side, so it contains 100 × 100 = 10 000 square centimetres; similarly 1 m² = 1 000 000 mm². So 25 cm² = 25 ÷ 10 000 = 0.0025 m².
caption: A square metre holds 10 000 square centimetres, not 100.

alt: A 600 N person in flat shoes (300 cm² = 0.030 m²) exerts 20 000 Pa on the floor. Balanced on one stiletto heel of 1.0 cm² (0.000 10 m²) the same force gives 6 000 000 Pa, 300 times more.
caption: Same force on 1/300 of the area gives 300 times the pressure.

alt: A 2.4 kg brick measuring 20 cm × 10 cm × 5.0 cm weighs 23.5 N. Standing on its 10 cm × 5.0 cm end (0.0050 m²) it exerts 4700 Pa; lying on its 20 cm × 10 cm face (0.020 m²) it exerts about 1200 Pa.
caption: The weight stays the same; the face in contact sets the pressure.

alt: A thumb pushes a drawing pin into a board. The same force acts on the large head, giving a low pressure on the thumb, and on the tiny point, giving a high pressure that drives the pin in. Large areas such as snowshoes and tractor tyres lower the pressure; small areas such as knife blades and needles raise it.
caption: For the same force, a smaller area gives a larger pressure.

alt: Water squirts furthest from the lowest of three holes in a tall container, because pressure increases with depth. A dam is thicker at the bottom where the water pressure is greatest. At a point in a liquid the pressure acts in all directions.
caption: Deeper or denser liquid means more pressure; shape does not matter.

alt: A diver 25 m below the surface of sea water of density 1030 kg/m³ experiences an extra pressure of 1030 × 9.8 × 25 = 252 350 Pa, about 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa, on top of atmospheric pressure. At 0.40 m the pressure due to oil (800 kg/m³) is about 3100 Pa and due to water about 3900 Pa; 49 000 Pa in water is reached at 5.0 m.
caption: Use the vertical depth below the surface and density in kg/m³.
